learn: The three levers of efficient serving: model, algorithm, system
Pruning (unstructured and structured) and the compression pipeline
Speculative decoding and its expected speed-up
Serving metrics (TTFT, TPOT, throughput) and cost per token
intro.why: Running an LLM for many users is mostly an exercise in moving fewer bytes and keeping the GPU busy. These techniques decide whether a product is affordable and responsive.

symbols: time to first token, time per output token

sections.title: Three levers of efficient serving
sections.plain: Make the model smaller, decode smarter, and run the system better.
sections.body:
Serving aims for low per-user latency, high total throughput and low cost per token, without losing quality. Three levers:

  1. Model compression: quantization, pruning, distillation. Fewer bytes per step attacks the bandwidth bound directly (M5).
  2. Decoding algorithms: speculative decoding produces several tokens per expensive pass.
  3. System and runtime: continuous batching, chunked prefill, paged KV memory, prefix caching, optimised kernels.

Every change must be checked against both speed metrics and a quality evaluation, since several levers are lossy.

sections.title: Quantization
sections.plain: Store numbers with fewer bits, like rounding prices to the nearest rupee instead of the paisa.
sections.body:
Quantization maps each weight to a b-bit integer and a shared scale:

$$s = \frac{\max|w|}{2^{b-1}-1},\qquad \hat w = s\cdot\text{round}(w/s)$$

Worked: a 1B-parameter model needs 4 GB in fp32, 2 GB in 16-bit, 1 GB in int8 and 0.5 GB in int4. Since decode is bandwidth-bound, halving bytes roughly doubles the decode-speed ceiling.

Error depends on granularity: one scale per tensor is crude; per-channel or per-group (e.g. 128 weights) scales track local ranges. Outliers are the main danger: one large weight or activation stretches the shared scale so small values round to zero (in code example ex1 a single outlier raises int4 per-tensor error from 0.19 to 0.99, while per-row scales stay at 0.15). Methods: post-training quantization with calibration (GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant), quantization-aware training, and 8-bit or 4-bit KV caches. Weights tolerate 4-bit well; activations are harder.

sections.title: Pruning and the compression pipeline
sections.plain: Remove the least useful weights, then let the model recover, then compress further.
sections.body:
Pruning removes weights judged unimportant (small magnitude, or small effect on the loss).

  • Unstructured: zero individual weights. High sparsity is possible, but dense GPUs only speed up with special patterns (e.g. 2:4 sparsity) or sparse kernels.
  • Structured: remove entire attention heads, channels or layers. The matrices shrink, so ordinary hardware runs faster, at a higher accuracy cost.

In ex1, pruning 30/50/80% of the smallest weights of a random layer gives output errors of 0.12/0.25/0.55: trained networks are usually more redundant than random ones, but the trend holds. A typical compression pipeline: prune → brief fine-tuning to recover → quantize → evaluate; distillation (M7) trains a small student on a large teacher's outputs as an alternative or complement.

sections.title: Speculative decoding
sections.plain: A small fast model guesses a few words ahead; the big model checks them all at once and keeps the ones it agrees with.
sections.body:
Because decode is bandwidth-bound, the big model can verify several tokens in one pass for about the cost of one. Speculative decoding: a cheap draft model proposes k tokens; the target model scores all k positions in parallel; tokens are accepted left to right with an accept/reject rule, and at the first rejection the target samples a corrected token. The rule makes the output distribution exactly the target model's.

$$E[\text{tokens per target pass}] = \frac{1-\alpha^{k+1}}{1-\alpha}$$

Worked: α = 0.8, k = 4 → 3.36 tokens per pass; α = 0.6 → 2.31. Speed-up also depends on the draft's cost. Variants use extra prediction heads (Medusa), the model's own earlier layers, or n-gram lookups in the prompt instead of a separate draft model.

sections.title: Continuous batching and chunked prefill
sections.plain: Refill a free slot the moment any request finishes, and slice long prompts so they don't hold everyone up.
sections.body:
Requests have very different output lengths. Static batching groups requests and waits for the longest to finish, leaving slots idle. Continuous (in-flight, iteration-level) batching schedules at every decode step: when a sequence ends, a waiting request joins immediately.

Worked (ex2): 64 requests, 8 slots: static 2,965 steps at 55% utilisation; continuous 1,816 steps at 90%, a 1.63× gain.

A long prompt's prefill can still stall ongoing decodes. Chunked prefill splits it into pieces processed alongside decode steps, smoothing latency. Some systems go further and run prefill and decode on separate GPU pools (disaggregated serving).

sections.title: Paged attention
sections.plain: Hand out cache memory in small blocks as needed, like an operating system does with RAM pages.
sections.body:
Reserving a contiguous KV region for the maximum length wastes memory, because most requests are far shorter (ex2: only 10% of slots reserved for 2,048 tokens were used). Paged attention (introduced by vLLM) splits the KV cache into fixed-size blocks, e.g. 16 tokens, allocated on demand and tracked by a block table; the attention kernel reads blocks wherever they are.

Waste falls to under one block per sequence (3.8% in ex2), so many more sequences fit, enlarging batches and throughput. Blocks can be shared copy-on-write, enabling prefix caching (shared system prompts) and parallel sampling from one prompt.

sections.title: Serving metrics and cost per token
sections.plain: Measure how quickly the first word appears, how fast words keep coming, how many words per second overall, and what each million words costs.
sections.body:
• TTFT (time to first token): queueing + prefill. Matters for interactivity.
  • TPOT (time per output token, or inter-token latency): decode speed per user.
  • Throughput: total tokens/s across users. Batching raises it but can raise TPOT.
  • Cost per token: hardware price divided by tokens produced.

Worked: a $2/hour GPU at 100 tokens/s produces 360,000 tokens/hour → $2 / 0.36M ≈ $5.56 per million tokens. Batched to 2,000 tokens/s: ≈ $0.28 per million. Services set latency targets (service-level objectives, e.g. TTFT under 500 ms at the 95th percentile) and maximise throughput within them.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Quantization is not free: check reasoning and long-context tasks, which can degrade before simple benchmarks do.
  • Speculative decoding helps latency most at small batch; at large batch the GPU is already busier and gains shrink.
  • Prefix caching makes repeated system prompts nearly free after the first request.
  • Tail latency (p95/p99) matters more to users than the average.

code.title: Quantization and pruning on a layer
code.explain: Prints memory for 1B parameters in fp32/16-bit/int8/int4 (4/2/1/0.5 GB), quantizes a random layer to int8 and int4 with per-tensor and per-row scales, shows a single outlier wrecking a shared int4 scale (error 0.99 vs 0.15 per-row), and measures the output error of 30–80% magnitude pruning.
mistakes: Using one scale for a tensor with outliers.
Expecting unstructured sparsity to speed up dense kernels.
code.notes: Random weights; trained models compress better.
code.code:
"""Quantization (fp32 -> int8 -> int4) and magnitude pruning on a random weight matrix."""
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
W = rng.normal(0, 0.02, size=(512, 512)).astype(np.float32)
x = rng.normal(size=512).astype(np.float32)
y = W @ x

N = 1e9
for name, b in (("fp32", 4), ("fp16/bf16", 2), ("int8", 1), ("int4", 0.5)):
    print(f"1B params in {name:9s}: {N*b/1e9:.1f} GB")

def quant(W, bits, per_row=False):
    qmax = 2 ** (bits - 1) - 1
    s = (np.abs(W).max(axis=1, keepdims=True) if per_row else np.abs(W).max()) / qmax
    q = np.clip(np.round(W / s), -qmax, qmax)
    return q * s
for bits in (8, 4):
    for per_row in (False, True):
        Wq = quant(W, bits, per_row)
        err = np.linalg.norm(Wq @ x - y) / np.linalg.norm(y)
        print(f"int{bits} {'per-row ' if per_row else 'per-tensor'} scale: relative output error {err:.4f}")

# One outlier weight ruins a shared scale
W2 = W.copy(); W2[0, 0] = 1.0
for per_row in (False, True):
    err = np.linalg.norm(quant(W2, 4, per_row) @ x - W2 @ x) / np.linalg.norm(W2 @ x)
    print(f"with one outlier, int4 {'per-row ' if per_row else 'per-tensor'}: error {err:.3f}")

# Magnitude pruning
for frac in (0.3, 0.5, 0.8):
    thr = np.quantile(np.abs(W), frac)
    Wp = np.where(np.abs(W) >= thr, W, 0)
    err = np.linalg.norm(Wp @ x - y) / np.linalg.norm(y)
    print(f"prune {int(frac*100)}% smallest weights: relative output error {err:.3f}")
print("unstructured zeros only save time with sparse kernels; structured pruning (whole heads/channels) speeds up dense hardware")

code.title: Speculative decoding, batching, paging and cost
code.explain: Tabulates expected tokens per target pass for α = 0.6/0.8/0.9 and k = 2/4/8, simulates static vs continuous batching (1.63× faster, 55% → 90% utilisation), compares contiguous vs 16-token paged KV allocation (10% used vs 3.8% waste), and computes $5.56 per million tokens at $2/h and 100 tokens/s.
code.notes: Simplified scheduler; real systems also handle prefill.
code.code:
"""Speculative decoding speed-up, continuous vs static batching, paged KV allocation, and cost per token."""
import numpy as np

# Speculative decoding: draft proposes k tokens, target verifies in one pass; each accepted with prob a
def expected_tokens(a, k):
    return (1 - a ** (k + 1)) / (1 - a)
for a in (0.6, 0.8, 0.9):
    print(f"acceptance {a}: " + ", ".join(f"k={k}: {expected_tokens(a, k):.2f}" for k in (2, 4, 8)) + " tokens per target pass")

# Static vs continuous batching: 8 slots, requests of random lengths
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
lens = rng.integers(20, 400, size=64)
slots = 8
static = sum(max(lens[i:i+slots]) for i in range(0, len(lens), slots))
free = [0] * slots
for L in lens:
    j = int(np.argmin(free)); free[j] += L
cont = max(free)
print(f"static batching: {static} steps; continuous batching: {cont} steps; speed-up {static/cont:.2f}x")
print(f"slot utilisation static {lens.sum()/(static*slots):.0%}, continuous {lens.sum()/(cont*slots):.0%}")

# Paged attention: reserve max length vs allocate 16-token pages
maxlen, page = 2048, 16
used = lens.sum(); reserved = maxlen * len(lens)
paged = int(np.ceil(lens / page).sum() * page)
print(f"KV slots reserved for max length: {reserved:,}; used: {used:,} ({used/reserved:.0%})")
print(f"paged (16-token blocks): {paged:,} allocated, waste {(paged-used)/paged:.1%}")

# Cost per token
price, tps = 2.0, 100
per_hour = tps * 3600
print(f"${price}/hour at {tps} tok/s = {per_hour:,} tok/h -> ${price/per_hour*1e6:.2f} per million tokens")
for tps in (500, 2000):
    print(f"  at {tps} tok/s (batched): ${price/(tps*3600)*1e6:.2f} per million")
